([support.apple.com](https://support.apple.com/guide/iphone/get-started-with-notes-iph9e04f3be2/ios?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Students who need memorization** | **RemNote** | Notes combined with flashcards and spaced repetition. |
| **Quick reminders and shopping lists** | **Google Keep** | Extremely simple, fast, and convenient for short-lived notes. |

### My recommendation

- Choose **Obsidian** if you want a durable, interconnected archive of ideas, research, journals, or work notes.
- Choose **Notion** if you want an all-in-one workspace or need to collaborate.
- Choose **Apple Notes** if you want something that works immediately with minimal setup.
- Choose **Google Keep** if most of your notes are short reminders.

**Bottom line:**  
**Obsidian is the best overall for power users; Apple Notes is the best for simplicity; Notion is the best for teams.**

samples.answer:
If **plain-text files are a hard requirement**, look for apps where the notes folder itself contains readable `.md` or `.txt` files—not merely an export feature. Markdown files are plain text and can be opened in any text editor.

## Best options

| App | Best for | File format | Platforms |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Obsidian** | Best overall knowledge base | Markdown `.md` files in a local folder | Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, Android |
| **Zettlr** | Open-source research and writing | Markdown and other text-based files | Windows, macOS, Linux |
| **QOwnNotes** | Lightweight notes with folders and syncing | Markdown `.md` files | Windows, macOS, Linux |
| **FSNotes** | Fast, native Apple note-taking | Markdown or plain-text files | macOS, iPhone, iPad |
| **Logseq OG/file version** | Outlining, daily notes, and backlinks | Markdown or Org-mode files | Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, Android |

### 1. Obsidian — best overall

Obsidian is the strongest default choice for most people. It stores notes as Markdown files in a folder called a vault, so you can edit them with another application or manage them directly in Finder/Explorer. It also offers backlinks, tags, search, graph view, templates, and a large plugin ecosystem. ([obsidian.md](https://obsidian.md/help/data-storage?utm_source=openai))

**Choose it if you want:**

- A polished, flexible knowledge base
- Wiki-style `[[links]]` and backlinks
- Lots of plugins and customization
- A large ecosystem and easy migration

**Caveat:** Obsidian’s features can encourage building an elaborate system instead of simply taking notes. Its files remain portable, but some plugins add app-specific metadata or syntax.

### 2. Zettlr — best open-source writing and research app

Zettlr is particularly good for long-form writing, academic notes, citations, and Zettelkasten-style organization. It works directly with folders of Markdown documents and can also handle plain-text files. Its workspaces are ordinary folders on your computer rather than a proprietary database. ([zettlr.com](https://www.zettlr.com/features?utm_source=openai))

**Choose it if you want:**

- Open-source software
- Research and academic-writing tools
- Citation and Pandoc integration
- A more document-oriented interface than Obsidian

### 3. QOwnNotes — best lightweight, traditional notepad

QOwnNotes is a good choice if you want something closer to a conventional notes application. It stores notes as plain-text Markdown files and lets you use ordinary folder-sync tools such as Nextcloud, Dropbox, or Syncthing. It is also designed to be relatively lightweight and supports Windows, macOS, and Linux. ([next.qownnotes.org](https://next.qownnotes.org/getting-started/concept.html?utm_source=openai))

**Choose it if you want:**

- A simple two-pane notes interface
- Minimal system-resource usage
- Nextcloud/ownCloud integration
- Less emphasis on plugins and graph-based organization

### 4. FSNotes — best for Mac and iPhone

FSNotes is a fast native Apple app that stores notes in portable Markdown or plain-text files rather than a proprietary database. It supports folders, tags, `[[links]]`, external editors, iCloud Drive, Dropbox, and optional Git backups. ([github.com](https://github.com/glushchenko/fsnotes?utm_source=openai))

**Choose it if you want:**

- A native macOS/iOS experience
- Fast capture and keyboard shortcuts
- Simple Markdown notes
- Notes that remain accessible outside the app

### 5. Logseq — best for outline-based thinking

Logseq is excellent if you prefer writing in bullets, daily journals, and deeply nested outlines. Its original **file-based version**, commonly referred to as Logseq OG, uses Markdown or Org-mode files. However, Logseq now has both a file-based version and a newer database-oriented version, so you should deliberately choose the file-based edition if portable files are important to you. ([logseq.io](https://logseq.io/page/b2ad9ce1-9cb7-4436-8083-54cb4516d324/df4dc09d-0a12-4c87-904e-22a9bf4c350a?utm_source=openai))

**Choose it if you want:**

- Daily notes and journaling
- Outliner-style writing
- Block references and backlinks
- An open-source alternative to Roam-style tools

**Caveat:** It is less natural than Obsidian or Zettlr for ordinary folder-based documents, and the file/database split makes its long-term format direction worth considering.

## My recommendation

- **Most people:** **Obsidian**
- **Open-source and research-focused:** **Zettlr**
- **Simple and lightweight:** **QOwnNotes**
- **Mac/iPhone user:** **FSNotes**
- **Daily journal and bullet-outliner workflow:** **Logseq’s file-based version**

If you want the **least lock-in possible**, use a folder of standard `.md` files, avoid app-specific plugins or metadata where practical, and back up or sync the folder independently of the app. Also note that file-sync services can create conflicts when the same note is edited simultaneously on multiple devices.

**My default recommendation: Notion.** It’s the best fit for scattered sticky notes, emails, and documents because you can keep everything in one searchable workspace, import Word/PDF/HTML/Markdown files, and save web pages with its browser clipper. ([notion.com](https://www.notion.com/help/web-clipper?utm_source=openai))

### Choose based on your habits

- **Notion — best overall for organization**  
  Good if you want notes, documents, projects, and databases together. Create one **Inbox** page for unsorted material, then organize it later.

- **Microsoft OneNote — best if you use Microsoft 365 or handwrite notes**  
  It feels like digital binders, supports web/PDF clipping, and its desktop app includes OCR for text in scanned images. ([support.microsoft.com](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/onenote/getting-started-with-the-onenote-web-clipper?utm_source=openai))

- **Evernote — best for capturing emails, scans, and documents**  
  Its feature set emphasizes web clipping, document/image search, PDF annotation, offline access, and emailing content into Evernote. ([evernote.com](https://evernote.com/en-us/compare-plans?utm_source=openai))

- **Obsidian — best for long-term ownership and connected knowledge**  
  Notes are stored as durable local files, with backlinks, search, properties, and a web clipper. It’s powerful but requires more setup. ([obsidian.md](https://obsidian.md/clipper?utm_source=openai))

### The simple system I’d use

1. Create an **Inbox**.
2. Put every new note, copied email, photo, or document there immediately.
3. Once a week, move items into only a few categories: **Projects, Reference, Personal, Archive**.
4. Use consistent titles, such as `2026-10-14 - Contractor estimate`.
5. Don’t overbuild folders—the search function should do most of the work.

**Bottom line:** Start with **Notion** unless you heavily use Microsoft products or handwritten notes; then choose **OneNote**. The system matters more than the app, so pick one and stop switching.

## Best overall: **Microsoft OneNote**

For most college students, **OneNote is the safest choice** because it combines:

- Separate notebooks and sections for each class  
- Typed notes, handwriting, drawings, equations, images, and PDFs  
- Strong support across Windows, Mac, iPhone, iPad, and Android  
- Easy sharing and collaboration

| Mostly type and want notes, tasks, calendars, and projects together | **Notion** |
| Use an iPad and Apple Pencil for handwritten notes/PDFs | **Goodnotes** |
| Want highly connected, research-oriented notes | **Obsidian** |
| Want automatic flashcards and active recall | **RemNote** |

**Notion** is especially good for organizing an entire semester—class notes, assignments, reading lists, and project plans—and its individual student Education Plan can be free with a qualifying school email. ([notion.com](https://www.notion.com/help/notion-for-education?utm_source=openai))

**Goodnotes** is usually better than OneNote for handwritten lecture notes, annotating slides, and writing equations on an iPad. Its features include handwriting tools, PDF annotation, audio synced with notes, and study sets. ([goodnotes.com](https://www.goodnotes.com/features/?utm_source=openai))

### My practical recommendation

- **Laptop or mixed devices:** OneNote  
- **iPad + Apple Pencil:** Goodnotes  
- **Mostly typed notes plus organization:** Notion  
- **Computer science, research, or long-term knowledge building:** Obsidian  

If you want only one answer: **start with OneNote**. It is flexible enough for nearly every major and less likely to become complicated than Notion or Obsidian.

**My top recommendation: Scrivener.**

For a long book project, Scrivener is usually better than a general note-taking app because it is designed around manuscripts: you can keep chapters, scenes, character notes, research, outlines, and drafts in one project. Its **Binder**, **corkboard**, **outliner**, split editor, snapshots, metadata, and export tools are particularly useful once a project becomes large. ([scrivenerprogram.com](https://scrivenerprogram.com/features?utm_source=openai))

### Choose based on your writing style

- **Scrivener — best overall for writing the actual book**  
  Choose this if you want to organize scenes and chapters, rearrange structure visually, track revisions, and eventually compile the manuscript into formats such as DOCX, PDF, or ebook files. ([scrivenerprogram.com](https://scrivenerprogram.com/features?utm_source=openai))

- **Obsidian — best for research-heavy or idea-driven books**  
  Choose this if your project involves many interconnected notes, sources, concepts, or world-building details. It stores notes locally, supports links between ideas, and includes Canvas for visually mapping research and story structure. ([obsidian.md](https://obsidian.md/canvas?utm_source=openai))

- **Notion — best for collaboration and project management**  
  Choose this if you need databases for sources, deadlines, interviews, tasks, or editorial collaboration. Its database views and relations are flexible, though it can feel less natural for drafting a long manuscript. ([notion.com](https://www.notion.com/help/category/databases?trk=article-ssr-frontend-pulse_little-text-block&utm_source=openai))

### A practical setup

For most authors, I’d use:

1. **Scrivener** for the manuscript, chapter outline, scenes, character sheets, and drafts.
2. **A reference manager** such as Zotero if the book is research-heavy.
3. Optionally, **Obsidian** for a large, interconnected research archive.

If you want **one app only**, use **Scrivener**. If you mainly need a place to accumulate and connect ideas before writing, use **Obsidian**.

Obsidian stores notes as Markdown-formatted plain-text files in a normal local folder called a vault. You can edit those files with other apps, manage them with your file manager, and sync them using services such as Dropbox, iCloud, OneDrive, Git, or Obsidian Sync. **Choose it if you want:**

- Backlinks, graph view, tags, search, templates, and plugins
- A large personal knowledge base
- Notes that remain portable and independently readable
- Desktop and mobile apps

**Caveat:** Obsidian-specific settings and plugins live in a `.obsidian` folder, and some advanced features depend on Obsidian-specific syntax or plugins.

### 2. Zettlr — best open-source option for serious writing

Zettlr works directly with workspace folders containing Markdown documents and explicitly avoids storing your notes in a proprietary database. It is especially strong for research, citations, Zettelkasten workflows, long documents, and exporting through Pandoc. ([docs.zettlr.com](https://docs.zettlr.com/en/first-time-users/workspaces.html?utm_source=openai))

**Choose it if you want:**

- Open-source software
- Local folders of ordinary Markdown files
- Citation and Zotero support

**Caveat:** It can feel more like a writing/research workbench than a lightweight notes app.

### 3. QOwnNotes — best “my files first” notebook

QOwnNotes stores every note as a local Markdown file, with no proprietary note database. It works offline and can optionally sync through Nextcloud or ownCloud. ([qownnotes.net](https://www.qownnotes.net/?utm_source=openai))

**Choose it if you want:**

- A simple folder-and-file model
- Open-source software
- No account or subscription requirement
- Easy backup with ordinary file-copy tools
- Windows, macOS, and Linux support

**Caveat:** Its interface and knowledge-management features are less sophisticated than Obsidian’s.

### 4. iA Writer — best for clean, focused writing

iA Writer is a polished writing environment that can organize and search local Markdown and plain-text files. Its documentation explicitly supports working with `.txt` and Markdown files, including files in local folders. ([ia.net](https://ia.net/writer/support/library/organize?utm_source=openai))

**Choose it if you care most about:**

- A distraction-free writing experience
- Excellent typography and editing
- Plain text and Markdown portability

**Caveat:** It is not as strong as Obsidian or Zettlr for backlinks, graph navigation, and complex note organization.

MarkText is an open-source, cross-platform Markdown editor with live preview, CommonMark/GitHub-Flavored Markdown support, math, front matter, and export features. ([github.com](https://github.com/marktext/marktext?utm_source=openai))

- A clean, lightweight Markdown editor
- Files that remain ordinary `.md` documents

### 1. Obsidian — best overall

Obsidian stores notes as Markdown plain-text files in a normal folder called a “vault.” You can edit those files with another editor, back them up with Git or a file-sync service, and migrate them to another Markdown application. ([obsidian.md](https://obsidian.md/help/data-storage?utm_source=openai))

**Strengths**

- Excellent linking, backlinks, search, graph view, tags, and plugins

- Works with ordinary `.md` files

**Trade-offs**

- Proprietary application, despite open file storage
- Some features rely on Obsidian-specific syntax or plugins
- Can become overcomplicated if you install too many plugins

**Choose it if:** you want the most capable general-purpose Markdown knowledge base.

---

### 2. QOwnNotes — best if “my files, my folders” matters most

QOwnNotes is explicitly designed around plain-text Markdown files. It can use an existing folder of text or Markdown files without importing them into a proprietary database, and it can optionally integrate with Nextcloud or ownCloud. ([qownnotes.org](https://www.qownnotes.org/getting-started/overview.html?utm_source=openai))

- Open source

- Lightweight and relatively straightforward

- Less polished and less visually flexible than Obsidian
- Smaller plugin and community ecosystem
- Primarily a desktop application

**Choose it if:** direct filesystem storage and open-source software matter more than flashy knowledge-management features.

---

### 3. Zettlr — best for research and serious writing

Zettlr is a Markdown-based writing and note-taking application aimed particularly at researchers, authors, and long-form writers. It works with Markdown files and supports citations, Zotero integration, Pandoc-based imports/exports, projects, and writing statistics. **Strengths**

- Open source
- Excellent for academic writing and long documents
- Citation and bibliography support

**Trade-offs**

- Less focused on visual knowledge graphs and backlinks than Obsidian
- Desktop only
- More writing-oriented than “quick capture” oriented

**Choose it if:** your notes are connected to research papers, citations, books, or substantial writing projects.

### 4. Logseq — best for bullets, daily notes, and outlining

Logseq is built around an outliner and daily-journal workflow. Its file-based setup works with local Markdown and Org-mode files. ([apps.apple.com](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/logseq/id1601013908?utm_source=openai))

**Strengths**

- Excellent for daily notes and meeting logs

- Strong block references and task workflows
- Open-source project

**Choose it if:** you naturally think in outlines, bullets, daily journals, and block-level references.

### 5. The Archive — best minimalist Zettelkasten app for Mac

The Archive manages a folder of plain-text notes and is deliberately software-agnostic. It is designed around search, tags, links, and a Zettelkasten-style workflow rather than folders or a large database. ([zettelkasten.de](https://zettelkasten.de/the-archive/help/?utm_source=openai))

It is especially attractive if you use Nextcloud, ownCloud, Syncthing, or ordinary folder synchronization. Its interface is more utilitarian than Obsidian’s, but that is partly the point. **3. Zettlr — best for research and serious writing**

Zettlr works with ordinary Markdown workspaces rather than storing your documents in a proprietary database. It has strong search, tags, linking, citation support, writing statistics, and export workflows. You choose the root folder, and it can work with folders synchronized by apps such as Dropbox, Nextcloud, or Syncthing. It is less of a full knowledge-management system and more of a dependable mobile text-file editor. nvUltra treats folders of plain-text MultiMarkdown files as its native storage model. Its distinguishing feature is a search-first workflow: you search for or create notes from the same interface. ([obsidian.md](https://obsidian.md/privacy?utm_source=openai)) | The app itself is not fully open source, and third-party plugins can introduce privacy risk. Use only trusted plugins. |
| **Standard Notes** | Sensitive notes with encrypted sync | End-to-end encryption, open-source encryption protocol and clients, offline use without an account, and optional self-hosting. ([standardnotes.com](https://standardnotes.com/help/1/who-can-read-my-private-notes?utm_source=openai)) | Less flexible for elaborate knowledge-management workflows; some advanced features require a paid plan. |
| **Joplin** | Open-source, self-hosted note-taking | Offline-first storage, Markdown support, multiple sync targets—including filesystem, WebDAV, Nextcloud, and Joplin Server—and optional end-to-end encryption. ([joplinapp.org](https://joplinapp.org/help/dev/spec/sync/?utm_source=openai)) | E2EE must be enabled and configured; the interface is less polished than some alternatives. |
| **Notesnook** | Polished privacy-focused experience | Local-first operation, offline editing, client-side encryption using XChaCha20-Poly1305, encrypted sync, and an open-source codebase. ([notesnook.com](https://notesnook.com/help/sync/how-sync-works?utm_source=openai)) | Full offline storage of attachments is a paid feature; attachments require an account to upload or sync. ([notesnook.com](https://notesnook.com/help/plans-and-limits?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Apple Notes** | Apple-only households | Convenient offline use and strong device integration; some locked notes and data types can receive end-to-end encryption through Apple’s security features. ([help.apple.com](https://help.apple.com/pdf/security/en_CA/apple-platform-security-guide-v.pdf?utm_source=openai)) | Less portable, less transparent, and not as attractive if you use Windows or Android. |

### My recommendations

- **Best overall for offline privacy:** **Obsidian**  
  Choose this if you want your notes to remain ordinary local files that you can copy, back up, encrypt, or manage with your own tools.

- **Best for private synced notes:** **Standard Notes**  
  Choose this if you want a simple app where the provider cannot read your synchronized note contents.

- **Best open-source/self-hosted option:** **Joplin**  
  Choose this if you want control over the sync destination, such as your own Nextcloud or WebDAV server.

- **Best balance of privacy and convenience:** **Notesnook**  
  It is more user-friendly than Joplin for many people while still offering encrypted sync and local-first operation.

### Important privacy distinctions

1. **Local storage is not the same as encryption.**  
   Obsidian’s local Markdown files are private from the service provider, but anyone who gains access to your unlocked computer can potentially read them. Use full-disk encryption and a strong device password.

2. **End-to-end encryption protects synced data, not necessarily your device.**  
   Standard Notes, Joplin, and Notesnook encrypt data before syncing, but an unlocked device, malicious plugin, or compromised operating system can still expose notes.

3. **Backups matter.**  
   Keep periodic encrypted backups—especially with Joplin or Obsidian. For Standard Notes and Notesnook, protect your encryption password or recovery key; losing both may make the data unrecoverable. ([notesnook.com](https://notesnook.com/help/backup-and-restore-notes-in-notesnook?utm_source=openai))

**Simple default choice:** start with **Obsidian** if you prioritize ownership and offline access; start with **Standard Notes** if you prioritize encrypted multi-device syncing.
